title: Marooned
statementMd:
![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e86604666aa3d1d2ed33744442c3d4259cc5f932.png)Image by the U.S. Navy, from commons.wikimedia.org

Konráð's hobbyist aeroplane, an on-board squat rack, and a banana peel have together produced what the aviation industry calls a rapid unscheduled disassembly. Konráð is now somewhere. The aeroplane is now everywhere.

He regained consciousness on a plank, the one part of the aeroplane still in one piece. Whether it is bobbing on the open sea or lying on dry land, he cannot tell in the fog. He did get one look at his GPS before it, too, gave up, so he knows exactly where he is.

Maybe he is in the middle of the ocean and needs to swim to land. The swim would be shorter if the Flat Earth Society were right, but Konráð has to make do with the Earth he has. Take it to be a perfect sphere of radius 6371 kilometres, with the origin of the coordinate system at its centre, so that every coordinate in this problem is a distance in kilometres. Take each landmass to be a polygon on the surface of that sphere, whose sides are great circle arcs. Konráð's Earth has no lakes, and therefore no islands in lakes either.

How far does Konráð have to swim?

## Input

The input consists of:

- One line with three real numbers x, y, and z, the position of Konráð.
- One line with an integer n (1≤n≤100), the number of landmasses.
- n descriptions of landmasses, each of which consists of:
- One line with an integer k (3≤k≤100), the number of corners of the landmass.
  - k lines, each with three real numbers x, y, and z, a corner of the landmass.

Every point in the input lies within 10−5 kilometres of the surface of the Earth, and is given with at most eight digits after the decimal point.

The corners of a landmass are given in the order in which they appear along its coast, with the land on the left — that is, counter-clockwise as seen from outside the Earth. Consecutive corners are joined by the shorter of the two great circle arcs between them; no two consecutive corners are antipodal. No two corners are within 0.1 kilometres of each other in a straight line. The landmasses are simple polygons, no two of them intersect, and none lies inside another.

## Output

Output the distance Konráð has to swim to reach the nearest landmass, measured along the surface of the Earth. If he is on land already, output 0.

Your answer should have an absolute or relative error of at most 10−5.
